newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: War-weary Tajiks face fight with shattered economy.
newsitem.headline: War-weary Tajiks face fight with shattered economy.

text.p: A senior International Monetary Fund (IMF) official urged Tajikistan on Monday to establish a transparent budget to restore an economy ravaged by four years of civil war.

"Economic policy must be played on clear rules and not on discretionary measures," Daniel Kaeser, an IMF executive director who monitors Central Asia, told reporters after meeting Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov.
Kaeser would not be drawn on what "discretionary measures" the embattled Tajik government has used.
But a worry for many of the former Soviet republic's six million population is the recent steep drop in the value of the national currency, the Tajik rouble.
There are no official statistics for inflation in the isolated, mountainous country bordering Afghanistan and China.
But the State Statistics Agency said earlier this year the government had printed 5.4 billion roubles in the first four months of the year, three times up on the same period in 1996.

Tajikistan's foreign exchange market -- effectively moneychangers with grubby satchels stuffed with wads of rouble notes -- have seen their value decline from 400 roubles to the dollar in April to around 600 on Monday.
A group of moneychangers descended on one car in a Dushanbe street like a flock of vultures, opening the door and thrusting money through the windows.
"I don't know why the rouble's fallen," said one wary moneychanger with a mouth full of gold teeth. "All I know is that when there are no buyers, the rouble goes down."
Kaeser said the IMF, which loaned Tajikistan $22 million last year to stabilise its currency, will send a mission to the Central Asian republic sometime this month.
"There needs to be a new credit arrangement," he said. "The Fund will also look closely at monetary policy."

Behind the rush to the dollar in Tajikistan lies local apprehension over the planned signing of a peace accord in Moscow this Friday which aims to end the civil war between Dusanbe's secular Russian-backed government and the republic's armed Islamic opposition.

"In a few days, an accord on peace and national reconciliation in Tajikistan will be signed which will open a new era in the life of the country," Zafar Saidov, the Tajik president's spokesman, said after the meeting with Kaeser.
But many peace deals in the past have led to more war and Tajiks are especially anxious over the proposed return of armed opposition fighters to the capital under a power-sharing accord.
The conflict has claimed tens of thousands of lives, although a ceasefire has largely held since December.
Even if peace is established, the Tajiks face a tough battle to rebuild a economy.
Local chieftains and armed bands fight over cash from Tajikistan's small gold production, aluminium smelting and a declining cotton crop.

According to the statistics agency, industrial production fell 10.8 percent in the first four months of this year compared to 1996 -- and this in the first few months of relative peace since war broke out in 1992.
Talk of economic reform is academic for most Tajiks until a real peace is secured.
"Nobody has any money," said a bored stallholder in one of Dushanbe's bazaars, explaining why business was slow.
